headline: Gulf oil shock, B.C.'s new government and Ontario's vote shaped the week
summary: Houthi missile barrages on Saudi Arabia and Trump's warnings about new Iran strikes pushed Brent to a six-month high near US$117 before easing to about US$110 Monday, feeding 3.1% Canadian inflation and bets on a Bank of Canada hike. Albertans rejected separation by roughly 75% to 25% (unofficial), Ottawa and Ontario unveiled $8.7 billion in tariff aid, Washington reshuffled its 50% tariff list, B.C. elected a Conservative majority, and Ontarians vote for mayors and councils today.

top.headline: Gulf attacks push Brent to a six-month high
top.what: Houthi barrages on Saudi Arabia and Trump's talk of new strikes pushed Brent to US$116.72 Friday, its highest since the spring; it was near US$111 Monday as regional security chiefs met in Tehran and U.S. intelligence warned of Iranian plots against Americans.
top.why: This is the single biggest driver of global energy prices this year.

top.headline: Canada inflation at 3.1% fuels Bank of Canada hike bets
top.what: September inflation rose to 3.1% on a 27.8% jump in gasoline, and August retail sales rebounded about 1.2%, so markets now price a strong chance of a hike to 2.50% on October 28.
top.why: Rates went from a debate about cuts to a likely hike in a matter of days because energy-driven inflation is spreading worries about expectations.

top.headline: Albertans vote about 75% to stay in Canada
top.what: About three-quarters of Albertans (CBC projected 76.5%) chose to remain in Canada versus roughly a quarter for starting a path toward a separation vote. Premier Danielle Smith said she will not hold another referendum on the issue while she is premier, but that grievances with Ottawa remain.
top.why: Even a non-binding result shapes national politics, federal-provincial relations and investor confidence in the energy sector.

top.headline: B.C. elects a Conservative majority
top.what: Lorne Doerkson's Conservatives won about 64 of 93 seats in unofficial results, ending nine years of NDP government; David Eby resigned as NDP leader.
top.why: A new B.C. government keen on LNG and scrapping the industrial carbon tax could reshape national energy and trade debates.

top.headline: Carney and Ford launch $8.7B tariff-aid plan
top.what: Ottawa and Ontario announced $8.7 billion, including $2.67 billion from the province, to modernize steel mills, help automakers shift to electric vehicles and build roads to the Ring of Fire mining region.
top.why: It is the first big joint federal-provincial answer to job losses from U.S. tariffs on steel and autos.

top.headline: Ontario votes; Tedjo projected to win Mississauga
top.what: Ontarians elected mayors and councils on Oct. 26; Alvin Tedjo is projected to win Mississauga while Toronto's Chow-Bradford race was still being counted Monday night.
top.why: City councils set property taxes, transit service, policing budgets and local housing approvals, and they last four years.

top.headline: U.S. reshuffles 50% tariffs as White House says deal is near
top.what: Washington swapped which Canadian goods face 50% tariffs, adding flooring, carpets and shampoos from October 30, and adviser Kevin Hassett said Sunday a deal is very close while blaming Alberta's separation push for delays. Earlier, Carney and Trump spoke at length amid a U.S. embassy accusation of meddling.
top.why: About three-quarters of Canada's exports normally go to the U.S., so any shift in tariffs hits Ontario jobs first.

top.headline: Forecasters tilt toward a Democratic House
top.what: About 21 million Americans have already voted, courts fought over voter-ID rules and DHS voter probes, and on Friday the Cook Political Report shifted 19 House races toward Democrats.
top.why: The result decides how freely Trump can act on tariffs, the Iran war and spending for the final two years of his term.
